lines: One single commit on the source database put an order and its three items into existence together, as one atomic act.
But nothing forces a consumer to read those two tables' own streams back in that same order, side by side.
So a join written as though they always arrive paired up finds, every so often, that the pieces showed up apart.
Think about what actually ties a row's own history together before you answer this.
A single row's changes carry something a split transaction doesn't: a key that every one of its own events shares.
Does a multi-table commit lose that same anchor the moment it gets divided, or does something else hold it together?
answer: Saying both break the same way ignores that one of them has an anchor the other one never gets.
A row's own key survives being split across however many events it produces; a transaction has no equivalent tag once its changes land in separate places.

lines: Here's the one fact that explains why a single row never loses its own place in line.
Every change event carries the primary key of the row it came from, stamped on it as its own identity.
Group a stream by that one field, and whatever order those grouped events arrived in is exactly the order they actually happened.
I measured that grouping claim against this sandbox's own real database, not a staged example.
Three separate rows each got updated three times, and I deliberately mixed up which row's update went out next.
Split by key afterward, every single row's own three values came back in precisely the order they were written, despite the scramble.
Now watch what happens the moment a transaction's own changes have to leave on two separate paths.
Each table gets routed to its own destination, so one commit covering two tables becomes two independent deliveries.
Nothing requires those two deliveries to be read back in the order they were originally written together.
I reproduced that exact split against the real database, using the identical commit from before.
One table's own delivery got drained in full before the other table's delivery had been touched at all.
Every item from that drained delivery still pointed at an order that, from this consumer's own view, hadn't shown up yet.
Losing that shared anchor isn't the end of the story, though, because the source still remembers it.
Two extra markers frame every commit: one announcing it has begun, and one announcing it is finished.
That closing marker carries a total count of events, broken down table by table, built straight from the transaction's own real position in the log.
I rebuilt that same split transaction's own identity directly from the slot's real numbers, not from guessing.
A consumer held every change aside by its own transaction number, instead of acting on each one right away.
The moment the count of held changes matched what that closing marker promised, the join released, and not one item was left waiting on an order that never arrived.
So here's where today's two measurements actually land, side by side.
One row's own order needs nothing extra, because its key already ties its history together on its own.
A transaction spanning several tables needs a consumer willing to wait for its own closing count before it treats anything as settled.
Here's a harder version of the same question to leave you with.
A transaction can land across several separate destinations at once, and none of those destinations knows anything about the others.
Whose responsibility is it, exactly, to put that transaction back together as one atomic act again?
answer: Each destination already keeps its own records in order on its own, but that guarantee stops dead at its own boundary and never reaches the next one over.
Rebuilding the transaction falls to whoever is reading all of those destinations, using the same opening marker, closing marker, and count this topic just measured.
